A_target.statement:
There is no [[Definition:Well-Formed Formula|formula]] $\map {\operatorname {True} } x$ in the language of arithmetic such that, for every sentence $\phi$:
:$\N \models \map {\operatorname {True} } {\ulcorner \phi \urcorner} \leftrightarrow \phi$

B_source.statement:
Let $\map B x$ be a formula with one free variable.
Then there is a sentence $G$ such that [[Definition:Robinson Arithmetic|Robinson arithmetic]] proves:
:$G \leftrightarrow \map B {\ulcorner G \urcorner}$

substitutions.the formula B: the negation of the putative truth predicate

object_map.reformulation: Diagonalize against the negated truth predicate to produce a sentence asserting its own falsity.

validity_conditions: Robinson arithmetic is true in N, so what it proves holds in N.
The theorem concerns definability of truth, not provability, so no consistency hypothesis is needed.
proof_plan:
By the [[Diagonal Lemma]] with $\map B x = \neg \map {\operatorname {True} } x$, there is $G$ with:
:$\mathsf Q \vdash G \leftrightarrow \neg \map {\operatorname {True} } {\ulcorner G \urcorner}$

As $\mathsf Q$ is true in $\N$:
:$\N \models G \leftrightarrow \neg \map {\operatorname {True} } {\ulcorner G \urcorner}$
